title: Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan: Miracle is Right
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the iHeart intro voice) profile Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan. The episode covers Helen's loss of sight and hearing at nineteen months, her family's appeal to Alexander Graham Bell and the Perkins School, Sullivan's own hard childhood and education at Perkins, the 1887 water pump breakthrough, Helen's education and Radcliffe degree, their vaudeville years, Sullivan's marriage and death in 1936, Helen's later trip to Japan, and her activism for socialism, women's rights, the ACLU and the NAACP. Listener mail from Danielle Greenberg about early remote work on IBM terminals closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts say they are long overdue to cover Anne Sullivan and Helen Keller and introduce the basic premise.

segments.title: Helen Keller's illness and early deaf-blind education
segments.summary: Helen lost sight and hearing at nineteen months. Deaf-blind people were often institutionalized and considered unteachable. Laura Bridgman was an earlier deaf-blind learner at Perkins, taught the manual alphabet by Samuel Gridley Howe.

segments.title: Anne Sullivan's childhood and education
segments.summary: Sullivan was partly blind, lost her mother and father's support, and lived in the Tewksbury poorhouse with her brother Jimmy, who died of tuberculosis. She was sent to Perkins at fourteen and graduated as valedictorian.

segments.title: Helen's family seeks help
segments.summary: When Helen was six, her parents sought help from Alexander Graham Bell, who advised them about Perkins. The family's Alabama background and finances are discussed.

segments.title: Sullivan arrives in Alabama and the March 1886 meeting
segments.summary: Sullivan arrived at the Keller home in Tuscumbia, Alabama, on March 3, 1886. She established discipline, and Helen's trust followed. Taking Helen outdoors helped calm her.

segments.title: The water pump breakthrough
segments.summary: Sullivan taught the word for water by spelling into Helen's hand at the pump. Helen understood language, and learned thirty words that day. Helen later learned braille and writing. A statue of the scene was unveiled in the Capitol Rotunda in 2009.

segments.title: Education, lip reading and Radcliffe
segments.summary: Helen studied at Perkins, at the Horace Mann School for the Deaf and with a speech specialist. She learned lip reading by touch. Sullivan prepared her for Radcliffe, where Helen graduated cum laude in 1904 as the first deaf-blind person to earn a college degree.

segments.title: Skeptics, fraud accusations and fame
segments.summary: Critics claimed the pair were a hoax. The hosts say the scrutiny confirmed their accomplishments. The two became world famous, meeting Rockefeller, Ford, presidents and Chaplin, and Mark Twain coined the Miracle Worker phrase.

segments.title: Vaudeville years and Polly Thompson
segments.summary: Sullivan married John Macy, whose marriage ended in divorce. The duo performed on the vaudeville circuit with assistant Polly Thompson from 1914, delivering inspirational talks and Q&A. They left the circuit in 1922.

segments.title: Complications, engagement and dependence
segments.summary: Sullivan and Helen were dependent on each other. Helen's engagement to Peter Fagan was blocked by Sullivan and Helen's parents. Radcliffe's admission was grudging, and Perkins leaders had questioned their legitimacy.
topics: Helen Keller relationship with Anne Sullivan

segments.title: Sullivan's death, Polly, and Helen's trips to Japan
segments.summary: Sullivan lost her sight fully by 1935 and died in 1936 of coronary thrombosis, and was interred at Washington National Cathedral. Helen wrote about sign language and her difficulty speaking clearly. Helen toured Japan in 1937-38 after Sullivan's death, and again in 1948 after World War II.

segments.title: Helen Keller's activism
segments.summary: Helen later became a social activist, supporting civil rights, the NAACP, the ACLU, socialism, the Industrial Workers of the World, women's suffrage, and birth control and venereal disease advocacy. Her books were burned by the Nazis.

segments.title: Closing remarks on Helen Keller
segments.summary: Hosts add final facts: Helen loved dogs, wrote books with a Braille typewriter, and remained an active writer. Helen died in 1968 and was buried alongside Sullivan and Polly Thompson at Washington National Cathedral.

segments.title: Listener mail: early remote work on IBM terminals
segments.summary: A listener named Danielle Greenberg recalls working remotely from home in 1983 on an IBM 3278 terminal with a 1200-baud modem, using the IBM Script program.

segments.title: Listener mail sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Danielle and invite more listener email.
